newsitem.title: ITALY: Iraq facing worst winter under sanctions - UNICEF.
newsitem.headline: Iraq facing worst winter under sanctions - UNICEF.

text.p: The head of the United Nations Children's Fund, UNICEF, said on Wednesday that low fuel and food supplies meant Iraq would probably face its toughest winter since sanctions were imposed six years ago.

"What we know is that we're coming into winter (and) given fuel supplies, given food supplies, given available resources, it is going to probably be the toughest winter they've gone through so far," Carol Bellamy, UNICEF's executive director, told Reuters in an interview.
"So we say again that it's those who are most vulnerable, who are children, who will suffer the most," said Bellamy, who is attending the U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit in Rome.
Bellamy, an American, said last month in New York that 4,500 children were dying each month in Iraq from hunger and disease.
Stringent U.N. trade sanctions were imposed against Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Humanitarian goods, such as those provided by aid agencies and charities, are exempted from the embargo. But Iraq has said that the impact of the sanctions on its infrastructure has added to a disastrous situation.
Iraq and the U.N. signed an agreement in May allowing Baghdad limited oil sales renewable every six months to raise money to buy urgent needs for the Iraqi population.
The pact was about to be implemented in September but was halted when Baghdad sent in troops to northern Iraq to help one Kurdish faction to fight against another.
Bellamy said all sides in disputes about sanctions - whether against Iraq, Cuba or other countries -- had to realise their effect on the most vulnerable members of the population.

"We are an organisation that tries to respond to people's needs. We think that sanctions, as a general matter, constitute the meat cleaver rather than the careful, thin knife. They are a very harsh approach," she said.

"They may be appropriate in one case and not in another case. We can't sit in judgment on that. What we say is that even if there are sanctions, (both sides should) understand that the implications may fall quite dramatically on those who are more vulnerable," she said.
Bellamy said these were often children and women.
"In Iraq, one could argue on the one side that the government should put more resources to its children...that is probably so in every country," she said.

"One could argue on the other side that sanctions have been very difficult on children (so) whatever you do -- Iraq's government and also those who support sanctions -- understand in both cases you have some responsibility to the children, so make some modifications to take into account the children," she said.
Pope John Paul, in an address which inaugurated the summit, said earlier that food insecurity was sometimes caused by "embargoes imposed without sufficient reasoning".
The Vatican has in the past criticised embargoes imposed on Cuba and Iraq, saying they hurt the poor most.
Criticism of sanctions also came from Libya's Agriculture Minister Ali Ben Romdhan, whose country has been hit by American and limited U.N. embargoes over its alleged role in terrorism.

"We are against this form of political pressure," Romdhan told Reuters. "We hope that this conference will help (achieve) the result that all boycotts are cancelled and are not used any more for political objectives," he said.
